rv.q: Happily, this revival starring Alastair Whatley, which arrives in London fresh from a few months’ touring, turns out to be neither cynical nor basement-bound.
There is a certain cheeky charm to all the clumsy cavorting, but it's too tame and obvious to feel properly subversive.
Thought-provoking, deeply moving and magnificently performed, The Importance of Being Oscar is theatre at its most intimate and affecting.
The script is brilliantly performed by Alistair Whatley who stands on a dark stage accompanied by two hoops of pure white light.

rv.q: Overall, this is an initially entertaining, then moving, evening, with Whatley casting a surprisingly sober regard in Oscar Wilde's direction.
Unfortunately, as a whole, the story can feel dramatically static, something the restrained tone and movement of Alastair Whatley's delivery, directed by Michael Fentiman, isn't able to overcome.
Alastair Whatley's efforts to recreate the one-man review at the Park Theatre is clearly a labour of love but proves a mixed, and not entirely satisfactory bag.
A collector’s item for Wilde connoisseurs and a moderately entertaining evening for everyone else.
For all the intelligence in Mac Liammóir’s writing, the material feels curiously remote from the wit and flamboyance of its subject.
The Importance of Being Oscar is incredibly touching and unfortunately still current and important in today’s shifting climate.
Alastair Whatley delivers a compelling performance that never lets your attention wander and fully does justice to this theatrical classic.
Whatley’s performance (supported by an excellent minimalist set and lighting) is near perfect.
Alastair Whatley takes the joy of the sorrow, and makes it his own.
Whatley works hard to capture the man's magnitude, offering a measured and poised depiction of one of Victorian Britain’s most exuberant characters.
Whatley’s adept though at invoking nuance and half-lit smiles, a world of covert celebration.
The Importance of Being Oscar is the definitive account of the downfall of a great man, and deserves to be seen, especially when approached as intelligently and carefully as it is in this production.
Alastair Whatley's assured performance gives it warmth, dignity, and humanity throughout.

If The Importance of Being Oscar sets out to inject some colour into the life of Oscar Wilde outside of the confines of his words, then a monochrome – and, sadly, mono tone – production only goes so far.
This is an engaging, vivid, emotionally and intellectually rich evening spent in the company of a true great.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this reverent one-man tribute to Oscar Wilde. While Alastair Whatley's performance earns praise, many find the production overly scholarly and restrained, prioritizing education over entertainment in its biographical approach.
